elements.text: Weyland Yutani Science Division

Thank you for volunteering for the Xenobiological Field Survey. If your participation was arranged on your behalf by the Debt Resolution Office, welcome all the same. Your enthusiasm is noted either way.

This manual covers the capture and containment of xenomorph queens. Inside you will find fabrication schematics for the necessary equipment, recommended field procedure, and the whole of what the Company has gathered on the species to date.
Read it before you need it. The sections are short because the situations they describe are short.
Everything that follows begins here. Royal jelly is drawn from the higher castes, and on its own it is a growth medium - it is what the hive feeds its young to push them up the ladder.
Introduce a poison to it and the jelly turns against its own purpose. Development stops. A specimen dosed with it does not advance, does not moult, and does not become the next thing.

Field specialists report moderate success brewing it into a potion, which sharpens the effect considerably. The Company neither endorses nor discourages the practice of drinking said potion, however we would appreciate it if notes can be taken.
It is also the active component of the inhibitor. Make more than you think you need.
The device that ends a queen's autonomy. Clamps to the neck.
Apply to a subdued queen. A solid mechanical clunk indicates the device has seated. A hiss indicates it has not, and that you have misjudged her condition.
Placed around the specimen and bound to her with chains.
Eight per fabrication. Mount them on any surface - floor, ceiling or wall - and position them before she arrives, not during.
A queen will take up to eight chains, but four hold her. Most field agents seat four, then use the spare set to reposition the first without ever letting her loose.
Runs from an anchor to the specimen. Two per fabrication.
It is not only for royalty. A chain takes hold of anything a lead will not - villagers included - and it is how an incapacitated queen is dragged anywhere at all. She does not walk to containment.
A chain announces itself as it binds. Count them. Three is not four, and three holds nothing at all.
Company tracking hardware, issued to the Survey on the understanding that it is returned with data. A tracker is clamped directly to a queen and reports her position for the remainder of her life.
Application
Applied by hand, to any queen, in any state. This is the one instrument in your kit that does not wait for her to be subdued - the inhibitor demands a helpless specimen, the tracker does not.
Personnel are reminded that walking up to an unrestrained queen and touching her is not made safe by the fact that the device permits it. The tracker has no opinion on your survival.
One tracker, one queen. The device is consumed on application.
A queen already carrying a tracker cannot be tagged again.
The unit is visible on the specimen once seated. You will be able to see, at a glance, which queens are on the register.
Labelling
Name the tracker on an anvil before you apply it and that name is what appears on the register. Left unnamed, she is filed by strain - "Aberrant Queen", or simply "Queen" for the common type.
The Survey strongly recommends naming them. A register of eleven entries all reading "Queen" is a register of nothing.
A note on permanence
A tagged queen will not quietly disappear from the world the way an untended specimen might. Once she is on the register, she stays. Consider this before tagging every queen you meet.
The reader. Where the tracker writes, the PDA reads - it queries the register and returns every tagged queen currently on file, with her position and the dimension she is in.
Use
Reusable. It is an instrument, not a consumable.
One unit serves the whole register. There is no need for a second.
Reports last known position, not live pursuit. She moves; the entry updates when she is observed.
When a signal is lost
A tracker goes dark for exactly two reasons, and the register records which.
Deceased. The specimen is dead. The entry is retained until you acknowledge it.
Interference. She has been taken into an empress emergence. The queen you were following no longer exists as a queen.

The second case is the one worth your attention. A signal that ends in interference is not a loss of equipment - it is notice that something considerably larger has happened at that location, and that the Survey would like to hear about it.
Do not simply throw a wild queen into your holding cell at base.

elements.label: Survey site 4 - structure loss following improvised containment

elements.text: Recovered survey imagery. The cell held for some hours.
We do appreciate the initiative, and the free data. It also remains the single most avoidable loss of materials and personnel across the entire survey.
She is not an ordinary specimen. While you study her, she is studying you.
Improvised containment of a wild queen leads her to treat the cell as raw material, and then the structure around it, until she has built her palace out of your base.
There are, however, measures you can take to subdue her correctly. They follow.
An unsubdued queen founds a hive. This is not aggression and it is not a response to you. It is simply what she does next, and she requires no permission to begin.

Founding is not a modest footprint. She claims territory considerably wider than the structure she excavates, carves chambers through whatever occupies the intervening space, and begins producing workers who widen it further. Your walls are not a barrier to this process. They are a duration.
Standing guidance
Subdue her before she settles, or keep her well away from anything you would mind losing.
A sealed room is not containment. It is a delay of uncertain length.
Only an inhibitor prevents founding. Nothing improvised has ever been observed to work.
The Company does not replace structures lost to preventable enthusiasm. It does, however, welcome the field notes.
A queen who has already founded can still be taken. Fitting an inhibitor severs her from the hive she made and reduces her claim to a single chunk of ground.

Be clear about what this does and does not achieve. The hive does not die with her removal — it is left queenless but functioning, and what has been excavated stays excavated. Capture stops the loss. It does not reverse it.
Act early. The difference between a five minute inconvenience and a permanent feature of your landscape is decided in the first few minutes of her life.
Every queen runs the same five stages between arrival and a working hive. Identifying the current one tells you how much time remains to you, which is the only figure that matters in the field.

left.text: Roughly five minutes. Mobile and hostile, but with no interest in territory yet.

elements.text: The longest uninterrupted window you will be given.

right.text: She commits to a site and travels to it, cutting through whatever lies between.

elements.text: Once she has chosen, she is working toward a hive and your window is closing.

left.text: She sleeps at the site for three days.

elements.text: A queen dispatched by an established hive skips this entirely. Assume the worst case unless you know her origin.

right.text: She wakes and begins to dig out her main chamber.

elements.text: This is the only excavation she performs herself. Her first drones appear during this stage. From here on the hive builds faster than you can control it.

left.text: She settles onto the ovipositor and begins to lay.

elements.text: She is no longer a wandering creature. She has claimed her throne as the hive's infrastructure.
A new queen is not full size. She arrives at roughly four fifths of her mature dimensions and moults up over about fifteen minutes, in three observable stages.
Left: fully moulted. Right: newly arrived.
Moulting occurs only when she is undisturbed. If she is moving, hunting, burning, injured, or has a target in view, she holds at her current size and waits for conditions to improve.
A moult in progress. She will not start one with you in view.
This is useful to you twice over. A queen who has been fighting is smaller than her age would suggest, and a queen still moulting is vulnerable in a way a mature specimen is not.
Observe her as you close the distance. Her size is a status report she cannot help but give you.
An inhibitor will only seat on a queen who cannot resist it. Five states qualify. Outside them the device will not attach, and no amount of persistence will change that.
Still growing. Any queen who has not finished moulting.
Incapacitated. Beaten down and unable to stand.
Hibernating. Asleep at her chosen site.
Fully restrained. Four anchors bound to her.
Hand placed. A specimen you introduced to the environment yourself, in any state.
Beaten down. She will rise again - three times in all - so the device goes on now, not after.

Attempt it on a healthy mature queen who is standing and unrestrained and she will hiss and shrug the device off. Personnel have reported this as equipment failure on more than one occasion. It is not. She simply is not beaten yet.
Growing

The cleanest window available and the one most often overlooked. A queen raised from a burster under your own supervision is vulnerable for the entire duration of her moult, and requires no confrontation whatsoever.
Hibernating
Three days of guaranteed opportunity. You must locate her first, and she is already at the site she has chosen to keep, which limits how much you will enjoy the result.
Incapacitated
Always available and always expensive. She can be put down three times. Budget accordingly.
Restrained
The deliberate method, and the only one that also yields a productive specimen. See Field Procedure.
The reliable approach, in order.
Prepare the site first. Anchors positioned, chains and inhibitor to hand.
Bring her to the site, or locate her hibernating.
Bind four chains. She is held once the fourth seats.
Fit the inhibitor. She is now Company property and will not found.
Four anchors, set before she arrives. Spacing is forgiving; the order you bind them is not.
A fully bound specimen. Three chains hold nothing - count them as they seat.

Beating her down also works and requires no preparation. It costs one of her three falls, and leaves her free the moment she recovers should you fumble the application. The Survey does not recommend it as a first approach, but records show it is the one most often used.

An inhibited queen is a contained breeder. Her hive autonomy is suppressed and her claim is capped to a single chunk. She will not excavate outward, will not commission chambers, and will not extend her territory.
She is not harmless. She still fights, and she still defends the ground beneath her. Contained is not tame, and the distinction has cost us personnel who assumed otherwise.
Build the walls
A chained queen is a beacon. Her own kind come to break her chains and will keep coming, and a rival strain comes to finish her - a helpless royal of another strain is a prize, not a prisoner.
Enclose the site. The chains hold her; they do nothing about what walks in after her.
The eggsack

Restrain an inhibited queen fully and she forms a chained eggsack and lays from it. She completes her growth to full size at that moment regardless of her age, so allow for the additional volume in your facility.
This is the outcome the Survey is after. A queen on an eggsack is production. A queen loose in your quarters is a demolition report and a difficult conversation.
A contained breeder on her sack. This is what the Survey is for.
